Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.

slides.say: a and b are positive integers, and a is bigger than b. When a is divided by seven, the remainder is two. When b is divided by seven, the remainder is five. What will be the remainder if a minus b is divided by seven?

So we know the remainders of a and b, and they ask for the remainder of their difference. And one of the choices says it can't be determined. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, writing each number as a tag, and then plugging in numbers.

[short pause] The letters k and m will count the complete groups of seven in each original number. The given remainders are the parts left outside those groups. Let's start with the tags. Remember, a number that leaves two when divided by seven is seven k plus two, full sevens plus two. And b is seven m plus five. Why m and not k again? a and b are different numbers, so they get different letters.

We want a minus b, so let's subtract the whole expression for b from the whole expression for a. Now subtract. a minus b is seven k minus seven m, plus two minus five. The sevens stay sevens, so seven times, in brackets, k minus m. And two minus five is negative three.

Negative three is the part we got after subtracting, but it isn't yet a valid remainder. We need to express that same number using a remainder between zero and six. But a remainder can't be negative. Dividing by seven, it's zero to six. So add the divisor, seven. Negative three plus seven is four. Why is that allowed? Adding a full seven never changes the remainder. Four leaves four, and eleven, four plus seven, leaves four too. So a minus b is full sevens, plus four, and the remainder is four, for every pair.

Let's check it with an actual division. Twenty-three leaves two, because three sevens are twenty-one. Twelve leaves five. Twenty-three minus twelve is eleven, and eleven divided by seven leaves four, because eleven is seven plus four.
So four, choice number four is our answer. And can't be determined is out, because it's four for every pair.
at: choice number four is our answer

slides.say: And what does that mean? Only the remainders matter. For a difference, subtract the remainders, two minus five, negative three. A negative result? Add the divisor. Negative three plus seven is four. For a sum, add them. Nine leaves two and twelve leaves five, and nine plus twelve is twenty-one, three sevens. Two plus five is seven, and that leaves zero, the same. For a product, multiply them. Nine times twelve is a hundred eight, fifteen sevens and three. And two times five is ten, which also leaves three.
Now careful with the order. A lot of students do five minus two, which is three, and that's choice number three, the trap. It's a minus b, so it's two minus five.

[pause] For this method, I'll choose actual values that obey the two remainder conditions and the condition that a is bigger than b. Now let's try plugging in numbers. I need an a that leaves two, so nine, which is seven plus two. And a b that leaves five and is smaller than a, so five itself. Nine minus five is four, and four divided by seven leaves four.

Now check the choices. Our example gives a remainder of four. But one choice says it cannot be determined, so an example alone does not settle that choice. We need to see what changing the numbers can do. Any other allowed a differs from nine by complete sevens. Any other allowed b differs from five by complete sevens too. Their difference can therefore change only by complete sevens, which cannot change the remainder of four.

So the remainder is always four, not just four for our example. That rules out cannot be determined. Choice number four is our answer. We can stop without trying more pairs. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number four is our answer
